content: The Burnet Institute in Melbourne, Australia, is home to Leanne Jones, a Research Associate affiliated with the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group Editorial Office at the University of Liverpool in the United Kingdom. Frances Kellie serves as the Managing Editor of the same group, while Myfanwy Williams is also a Research Associate within the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group at the University of Liverpool. The External Review Group (ERG) includes Ayse Akin from the Department of Public Health at Baskent University in Ankara, Turkey, and Justus Hofmeyr, who is associated with the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at the University of Botswana in Gaborone, Botswana, as well as the University of the Witwatersrand and Fort Hare in East London, South Africa. Tina Lavender, from the Centre for Global Women’s Health at the University of Manchester’s School of Nursing, Midwifery, and Social Work in the United Kingdom, is also a member. Suneeta Mittal, from the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at Fortis Memorial Research Institute in Haryana, India, and Alan Tita, from the Maternal-Fetal Medicine Division and Center for Women’s Reproductive Health at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, USA, contribute to the group. Khalid Yunis, a Professor of Pediatrics and Head of the Division of Neonatology at the American University of Beirut in Lebanon, is also part of the ERG. John Varallo, the Global Director of Safe Surgery at Jhpiego, an affiliate of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, USA, is another key member. The World Health Organization (WHO) Country and Regional Officers include Bremen De Mucio, who focuses on sexual and reproductive health at the WHO Regional Office of the Americas in Montevideo, Uruguay; Karima Gholbzouri, who works in the Eastern Mediterranean Regional Office in Cairo, Egypt; Chandani Anoma Jayathilaka, who specializes in family health and gender at the South-East Asia Regional Office in New Delhi, India; Oleg Kuzmenko, who is part of the Division of Country Health Programs at the European Regional Office in Copenhagen, Denmark; Leopold Ouedraogo, who focuses on reproductive and maternal health at the African Regional Office in Brazzaville, Democratic Republic of the Congo; and Howard Sobel, who works on maternal, newborn, child, and adolescent health at the Western Pacific Regional Office in Manila, Philippines. Claudio Sosa, from the WHO Regional Office of the Americas, also contributes to sexual and reproductive health initiatives. The WHO Steering Group includes experts such as Mercedes Bonet, Doris Chou, Tina Lavin, Olufemi T. Oladapo, Joshua P. Vogel, and Maurice Bucagu, who focus on maternal and perinatal health within the Department of Sexual and Reproductive Health and Research. Christine Francis, a consultant in the Department of Surveillance, Prevention, and Control, also plays a role in these efforts. The WHO recommendations on the choice of antiseptic agents and methods for preoperative skin preparation for cesarean sections prioritize outcomes such as severe infectious morbidity (e.g., sepsis, septic shock, laparotomy, or hysterectomy due to infection), puerperal infections (e.g., endometritis with or without myometritis or salpingitis), and surgical site infections. Additional important outcomes include maternal death, cost of care, allergic reactions at the operation site, maternal satisfaction, maternal well-being, neonatal infections, and severe neonatal morbidity. These outcomes were updated to align with the current WHO definition of maternal sepsis, and new outcomes such as maternal satisfaction and well-being were added. Evidence on the effectiveness of different antiseptic agents and application methods for preoperative skin preparation was derived from a Cochrane systematic review of 13 trials involving 6,938 women. The trials compared agents such as chlorhexidine gluconate (CHX) with alcohol versus povidone-iodine (PVP-I) in aqueous or alcohol-based solutions, parachlorometaxylenol with PVP-I versus PVP-I alone, and isopropyl alcohol scrub plus iodophor-impregnated drapes versus iodophor scrub alone. The trials varied in their methods, settings, and definitions of surgical site infections, with most studies conducted in the USA, Egypt, India, Indonesia, and Nigeria. The review found that CHX with alcohol may reduce surgical site infections compared to PVP-I, but the evidence was of low certainty. Subgroup analyses by solution type (alcohol-based versus aqueous-based) did not show significant differences, but the small number of studies and imbalanced subgroup sizes limited the reliability of these findings. Other comparisons, such as parachlorometaxylenol with PVP-I versus PVP-I alone, and isopropyl alcohol scrub plus iodophor-impregnated drapes versus iodophor scrub, also showed very low certainty evidence regarding their effectiveness in reducing infections. The panel recommended alcohol-based antiseptic solutions containing CHX for surgical site skin preparation in patients undergoing cesarean sections, based on low to moderate quality evidence. However, the certainty of evidence on cost-effectiveness, maternal satisfaction, and well-being remains limited. The intervention is likely to increase health equity by preventing severe health consequences of peripartum infections, especially in low-resource settings, but challenges such as the availability of high-quality antiseptic solutions may limit its full benefits. The acceptability of the intervention is high among healthcare providers, as it aligns with common clinical practices. However, cultural and religious considerations, such as the use of alcohol-based agents, may require engagement with community leaders to address potential barriers.
